subject: history
title: Feudalism in Medieval Europe
welcome_lead: Step into a world of fiefs, vassals and three-field rotations as medieval Europe organised itself around mutual obligation.
meta_desc: History Society & Economy 750-1400 Adventure 1: feudalism, manorialism and the medieval social order.
final_note: You have surveyed the manor and the fief. The medieval economy was richer and more dynamic than the cliché of 'Dark Ages' suggests.

concepts.def: System of political and military relationships in which lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in return for service.
Economic system organising agricultural production around the lord's manor and peasant labour.
Estate granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for homage and military service.
Unfree peasant tied to the land of a manor, owing labour and dues to a lord.
Crop rotation in which a third of arable land lay fallow each year, increasing productivity from c.800 onward.
Formal act in which a vassal pledged loyalty and service to a lord.

walkthroughs.body_html: Following the Carolingian period, western Europe developed a layered hierarchy in which kings granted land to great magnates, who in turn enfeoffed knights. Each tier owed military and political services upward and offered protection downward. The bulk of the population — free and unfree peasants — lived on manors, working the lord's demesne in addition to their own strips.

The manor combined arable, meadow, woodland and waste, often using the open-field system. Adoption of the heavy plough, horse collar and three-field rotation expanded output between roughly 1000 and 1300, supporting population growth, the rise of towns and a more monetised economy.

The thirteenth century saw the commutation of labour services into money rents in many regions. The catastrophe of the Black Death (1346-53) accelerated this trend by creating labour scarcity and increasing peasant bargaining power, contributing to revolts such as the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the gradual decline of serfdom in western Europe.

A military rank in the king's guard
A type of medieval coin
A church court

Hybrid wheat

mcqs.q: How did Anglo-Saxons come to dominate post-Roman Britain?
options: The 1905 Revolution was led by Lenin from the Winter Palace.
A mix of migration from northern Germany and Denmark, settlement and intermarriage, and cultural absorption of Romano-British populations — not simple invasion and replacement.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.
Anglo-Saxons invaded Britain and wiped out all the Romano-British inhabitants.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.
The 1905 Revolution was led by Lenin from the Winter Palace.
The 1905 Revolution achieved nothing because the Tsar stayed in power.
It failed to overthrow the Tsar but forced the October Manifesto creating the Duma, exposing autocracy's weaknesses and rehearsing the structures of 1917.

mcqs.q: What was the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559?
options: Elizabeth made England fully Protestant and banned Catholic worship outright.
Elizabeth reunited England with the Pope to make peace with Spain.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.
A deliberate via media — a Protestant doctrine and English-language prayer book combined with some Catholic-style ceremony — designed to maximise conformity.
